sudan.content: تحركات حكومية لتأمين الوقود والكهرباء وتمويل المحطات المتضررة من القصف - سودان تربيون تخطى الى المحتوى من نحن اتصل بنا English الإثنين , 2 نوفمبر - 2026 سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية الأخبار تحركات حكومية لتأمين الوقود والكهرباء وتمويل المحطات المتضررة من القصف الأخبار تحركات حكومية لتأمين الوقود والكهرباء وتمويل المحطات المتضررة من القصف 2 نوفمبر 2026 في الأخبار , الحرب بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع , الخرطوم , السودان 0 مسيرات استهدفت محطة توليد في حلفا الجديدة - الإثنين 2 نوفمبر 2026 الخرطوم 2 نوفمبر 2026- كثفت الحكومة السودانية تحركاتها لمواجهة تداعيات استهداف منشآت الطاقة والكهرباء، عبر خطط عاجلة لتأمين إمدادات الوقود وتقليل ساعات القطع الكهربائي. وكشف وزير الطاقة والنفط، المعتصم إبراهيم أحمد، عن تدابير تعمل الوزارة على تنفيذها للحد من أزمة الوقود والكهرباء، مؤكداً أن الوزارة في حالة طوارئ وتعمل على توفير بدائل طاقية تضمن استمرار الإمداد، رغم الأضرار التي لحقت بعدد من منشآت قطاع الطاقة والكهرباء جراء الاستهدافات المتكررة. وقال الوزير، خلال مقابلة مع التلفزيون العربي، إن الوزارة بدأت تنفيذ خطة طوارئ لإعادة تأهيل المحطات والمنشآت المتضررة واستعادة الخدمات والحد من تداعيات الأضرار، بما يسهم في الحفاظ على استقرار الإمدادات ومواصلة تقديم الخدمات للمواطنين. وأشار إلى أن الوزارة تعمل على تقليل ساعات القطع الكهربائي بصورة تدريجية إلى حين اكتمال برامج الصيانة، لافتاً إلى ارتفاع تكلفة عمليات الإصلاح والوقت الذي تتطلبه، في وقت تحدث فيه عن تحسن في الإمداد، وتوقع انفراج أزمة الوقود خلال الأيام المقبلة. وأوضح المعتصم أن هناك برمجة لعمليات الاستيراد والإمداد، مشيراً إلى وصول عدد من البواخر وبدء تفريغ حمولاتها وتوزيعها على محطات الخدمة، مع تأمين عمليات التوزيع والعمل على انتظامها. وفي سياق متصل، عقد وزير الدولة بوزارة المالية، محمد نور عبد الدائم، اجتماعاً موسعاً بمكتبه بالوزارة، مع ممثلي البنك الدولي وبنك التجارة والتنمية للكوميسا (TDB)، المنفذ لمشروع (Ascent)، لبحث إيجاد حلول عاجلة لتمويل المحطات التي خرجت عن الخدمة جراء الاستهدافات الأخيرة التي طالت البنية التحتية للطاقة ومحطات الكهرباء العامة. وتناول الاجتماع بصورة عاجلة سبل الحد من تأثير الأضرار على الموسم الزراعي الشتوي في المناطق المتضررة، إلى جانب دراسة توفير حلول بديلة للطاقة بالتعاون مع البنك الدولي وشركائه الدوليين، بما يضمن استمرار المشروعات الزراعية وعدم تعطلها. ومنذ أكثر من أسبوع، تواجه محطات الكهرباء في معظم أنحاء السودان استهدافاً ممنهجاً بالمسيّرات، حيث تعرضت نحو 18 محطة لتوزيع الكهرباء في ولايات القضارف والخرطوم والجزيرة والبحر الأحمر، فضلاً عن سنار والنيل الأبيض وجنوب كردفان ونهر النيل والشمالية وكسلا، لهجمات وأضرار بالغة تسببت في انقطاع التيار الكهربائي عن عدد من المدن وتأثر قطاعات حيوية. الكلمات: أزمة الكهرباء في السودان أزمة الوقود استهداف منشآت الطاقة البنك الدولي الخرطوم السودان الكوميسا محطات sudan.content: مصر والسودان يدعوان إثيوبيا لتغيير سياستها بشأن سد النهضة | أخبار | الجزيرة نت تخطى إلى المحتوى الرئيسي الجزيرة تصفح في التطبيق حمل التطبيق البث الحي الرئيسية أخبار اقتصاد رياضة رأي ميدان متخصصة محليات فيديو الحساب البث الحي فلسطين انتخابات أمريكا اليمن إيران أخبار السودان مصر والسودان يدعوان إثيوبيا لتغيير سياستها بشأن سد النهضة 2 نوفمبر 2026 حفظ شارِكْ وقت القراءة: 3 دقائق جانب من اجتماع وزراء الخارجية والري في مصر والسودان (وزارة الخارجية المصرية) استمع 4:44 0:00 4:44 3:23 أعلنت مصر والسودان ، اليوم الاثنين، رفضهما لأي تحركات "أحادية" في حوض النيل الشرقي، ودعوة إثيوبيا إلى تغيير سياستها بشأن سد النهضة . وقالت الدولتان، في بيان مشترك عقب محادثات ثنائية جمعت وزراء الخارجية والري في البلدين، إنهما تتفقان في أن "سد النهضة الإثيوبي الأحادي المخالف للقانون الدولي تترتب عنه آثار جسيمة، ويمثل تهديدا مستمرا لدولتي مصب نهر النيل في ظل الإدارة الإثيوبية الأحادية للسد، وغياب آلية قانونية مُلزمة لحوكمته". أخبار مقترحة مياه تنحسر وجزر تظهر.. كيف تغيّر مجرى النيل الأزرق وسط السودان خلال عام؟ مُسيرات الدعم السريع تضرب الطاقة.. رسائل تتجاوز الميدان وبينما نبّه البيان إلى رفض الدولتين محاولة إثيوبيا إقحام بقية دول حوض النيل في هذه القضية، أكد رفض أي نفاذ بحري لأي دولة غير مشاطئة للبحر الأحمر على حساب سيادة الدول المشاطئة ووحدتها وسلامة أراضيها وموانئها، ورفض أي محاولات لاستغلال الأوضاع الإقليمية لعسكرة البحر الأحمر ، أو اتخاذ إجراءات أحادية تمس سيادة ووحدة أراضي دول الإقليم. الدفاع عن الأمن المائي كما شدد على ضرورة الدفاع عن الأمن المائي لدولتي مصب نهر النيل، والحفاظ على حقوق واستخدامات البلدين المائية كاملة بموجب اتفاقية 1959. ودعا البيان إثيوبيا إلى تغيير سياستها الأحادية، واستعادة التعاون وفقا للقواعد واجبة التطبيق للقانون الدولي. وفي شأن آخر، أكد الجانبان رفضهما أي تهديد لوحدة وسلامة السودان، مشيرين إلى عزمهما على تعزيز التنسيق المشترك من أجل استعادة الاستقرار في هذا البلد. وأدان البيان: "استهداف المليشيات المتمردة للبنية التحتية بجمهورية السودان خاصة محطات الكهرباء والمنشآت المائية، من خلال إطلاق مسيّرات من إحدى دول الجوار"، في إشارة إلى قوات الدعم السريع التي تخوض قتالا ضد الجيش السوداني. وزراء الخارجية والري في مصر والسودان (وزارة الخارجية المصرية) رفض إنشاء كيانات موازية كما شدد البيان على "الرفض القاطع لإنشاء أي كيانات موازية أو الاعتراف بها، باعتبار أن ذلك يمس وحدة السودان وسلامة أراضيه، والحفاظ على مؤسسات الدولة السودانية ومنع المساس بها". ويشكّل ملفا سد النهضة ودعم أديس أبابا عسكريا لقوات الدعم السريع عوامل توتر في العلاقة بين السودان وإثيوبيا، إذ أعلنت، الخرطوم ، أمس الأحد، إيداع شكوى ضد إثيوبيا لدى كل من مجلس الأمن الدولي ومجلس السلم والأمن الأفريقي على خلفية الاعتداء من داخل أراضيها على مواقع وأعيان مدنية ومحطات كهرباء في السودان. وقال مجلس السيادة السوداني إن أكثر من 180 طائرة مسيّرة تابعة لقوات الدعم السريع هاجمت السودان، خلال العام الجاري، انطلاقا من داخل الأراضي الإثيوبية. ومنذ أبريل/نيسان 2023، تتحارب قوات الدعم السريع و الجيش السوداني بسبب خلاف بشأن المرحلة الانتقالية، مما تسبب في مقتل عشرات آلاف السودانيين ونزوح نحو 13 مليونا. المصدر: الصحافة المصرية حفظ شارِكْ حول هذه القصة السودان يشكو إثيوبيا الهجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة على البنية التحتية الحيوية للطاقة في السودان، مما تسبب في انقطاع واسع النطاق للكهرباء وتعطيل الخدمات الأساسية وإمدادات المياه النظيفة، فيما يواصل السكان الفرار من ديارهم بحثا عن الأمان. وفي مؤتمره الصحفي اليومي، نقل ستيفان دوجاريك المتحدث باسم الأمين العام، قلق مكتب الأمم المتحدة لتنسيق الشؤون الإنسانية (أوتشا) إزاء هذه الهجمات وتداعياتها على السكان في عدد من الولايات السودانية. وبحسب التقارير، استهدفت غارات بطائرات مسيّرة اليوم محطتين لتوليد الكهرباء في ولاية كسلا، ومحطة فرعية في مروي. وطالت هجمات أمس مرافق كهربائية في ولاية نهر النيل، فيما استُهدفت يوم السبت محطة فرعية في ولاية البحر الأحمر، إلى جانب مواقع في شمال كردفان وولاية الجزيرة. تعطل المياه النظيفة ومخاطر انتشار الأمراض وأكد شركاء الأمم المتحدة في العمل الإنساني أن انقطاع الكهرباء ونقص الوقود أديا إلى تعطل إمدادات المياه النظيفة، مما اضطر السكان إلى الاعتماد على مصادر مياه غير معالجة، وهو ما يزيد من مخاطر الإصابة بالأمراض المنقولة عبر المياه. وأشار دوجاريك إلى أن الهجمات لا تزال مستمرة، وأشار إلى إدانة الأمين العام الشديدة لتصاعد هجمات المسيّرات التي تنفذها أطراف النزاع. وكان الأمين العام قد ذكر، في بيان صدر قبل يومين ، أن هذه الهجمات تسببت في مقتل مئات المدنيين، بينهم نساء وأطفال، في أنحاء السودان ومنطقة أبيي، في انتهاك صارخ للقانون الدولي الإنساني. وأعرب عن استيائه البالغ إزاء الهجمات التي تستهدف المدنيين والبنية التحتية الحيوية التي يعتمدون عليها، بما فيها المرافق الصحية. ودعا الأطراف إلى الاتفاق فورا على وقف الأعمال العدائية والانخراط بحسن نية في جهود الوساطة، بما فيها الجهود التي يقودها مبعوثه الشخصي للسودان، بيكا هافيستو. استمرار النزوح في دارفور والنيل الأزرق وفي شمال دارفور، يواصل السكان الفرار من ديارهم بحثا عن الأمان. وتقدّر المنظمة الدولية للهجرة أن نحو ألفي شخص نزحوا من قريتي كانو وبارو خلال الأسبوع الماضي. أما في ولاية النيل الأزرق، فقد نزح ما يقرب من 120 ألف رجل وامرأة وطفل بين كانون الثاني/يناير ومنتصف الشهر الماضي. وجدد المتحدث باسم الأمين العام الدعوة إلى حماية المدنيين واحترام القانون الدولي الإنساني، والسماح للعاملين في المجال الإنساني بإيصال المساعدات حيثما ومتى تشتد الحاجة إليها. هافيستو يعتزم العودة إلى السودان وعلى صعيد الجهود الدبلوماسية، أفاد دوجاريك بأن بيكا هافيستو اختتم أمس زيارة استغرقت يومين إلى المنامة في البحرين، شارك خلالها في "حوار المنامة" الذي نظمه المعهد الدولي للدراسات الاستراتيجية. وعقد هافيستو على هامش الحوار لقاءات مع عدد من المسؤولين، بينهم وزير خارجية البحرين. وجاءت الزيارة عقب مشاركته الأسبوع الماضي في منتدى أديس أبابا والاجتماع السنوي للمبعوثين الإقليميين إلى منطقة القرن الأفريقي. ويعتزم هافيستو العودة إلى السودان خلال الأسابيع المقبلة لمواصلة التواصل مع الأطراف المعنية الرئيسية، بما فيها السلطات السودانية، لبحث والدعم السريع , السودان , دارفور 0 معظم الأطفال والنساء الوافدين من الفاشر إلى طويلة يعانون من سوء التغذية - ارشيف الخرطوم 2 نوفمبر 2026 – كشفت منظمة الأمم المتحدة للطفولة “يونيسف” ومجموعة التغذية، الاثنين، عن تجاوز عتبة الطوارئ التي حددتها منظمة الصحة العالمية عند 15% في 49% من مسوحات التغذية التي أُجريت في السودان خلال عام 2026. ويحتاج 8.4 ملايين سوداني إلى مساعدات التغذية خلال هذا العام، منهم 4. 19 ملايين شخص يُتوقع أن يعانوا من سوء التغذية الحاد، من بينهم 824, 827 طفلاً، بحسب الأمم المتحدة. وقالت يونيسف ومجموعة التغذية، في تقرير يغطي الفترة من يناير إلى سبتمبر، إن “18 من أصل 37 مسحاً تغذوياً، بما يعادل 49% من المسوحات، أظهرت انتشاراً لسوء التغذية الحاد عند عتبة الطوارئ، فيما سجلت 7 مسوحات نسباً تبلغ 20% أو أكثر”. واعتبر الترير أن الوضع التغذوي في دارفور هو الأكثر حدة، حيث تجاوزت 13 من أصل 17 مسحاً أُجريت في الإقليم عتبة الطوارئ. وأشار إلى أن 5 من أصل 20 مسحاً أُجريت في تلكوك بولاية كسلا، وأم بدة وأم درمان في الخرطوم، والرهد في القضارف، وجبرة الشيخ في شمال كردفان، تجاوزت عتبة الطوارئ. وأفاد بأن المسوحات المنفذة في النيل الأزرق وسنار وجنوب كردفان ووسط دارفور والنيل الأبيض لم تتخطَّ عتبة الطوارئ. ويُقدّر قطاع التغذية التابع للأمم المتحدة أن يحتاج 8.4 ملايين من الأطفال دون سن الخامسة والنساء الحوامل والمرضعات في 2026 إلى مساعدات التغذية، منهم نحو 5 ملايين طفل دون سن الخامسة و3.4 ملايين من الحوامل والمرضعات. ويحتاج 4.19 ملايين شخص إلى خدمات علاج سوء التغذية الحاد خلال هذا العام، من بينهم نحو 825 ألف طفل دون سن الخامسة يعانون من سوء التغذية الحاد الوخيم، و2.76 مليون شخص يعانون من سوء التغذية الحاد المتوسط، و599,681 من الحوامل والمرضعات. وتمثل ولايات الخرطوم وشمال دارفور وجنوب دارفور والجزيرة 42% من إجمالي عبء سوء التغذية، بينما تمثل ولايات دارفور الخمس 30% من العبء الإجمالي، فيما تمثل ولايات كردفان الثلاث 15%. معدل الاستجابة وقال التقرير إن فريق تنسيق قطاع التغذية حشد أكثر من 53 شريكاً لتوسيع التدخلات العلاجية والوقائية، مع وجود نحو 2,500 مركز لبرنامج التغذية العلاجية الخارجية، وما بين 113 و130 مركزاً للتغذية العلاجية الداخلية. وأوضح أن عدد الأطفال الذين تلقوا العلاج من سوء التغذية الحاد الوخيم دون مضاعفات طبية عبر برنامج التغذية العلاجية الخارجية بلغ 383,155 طفلاً خلال الأشهر التسعة الأولى، بما يعادل 80.6% من المستهدف البالغ 475,231 طفلاً. وأفاد بأن مراكز التغذية العلاجية الداخلية المخصصة للأطفال المصابين بسوء التغذية الحاد المصحوب بمضاعفات طبية سجلت 26,016 حالة قبول، بما يعادل 37.2% من المستهدف البالغ 69,966 حالة. وذكر التقرير أن 61 محلية لم تسجل أي حالات قبول في مراكز التغذية العلاجية الداخلية، رغم وجود احتياجات مقدرة للعلاج، ما يعكس فجوات في توفر هذه الخدمات. وأشار إلى أن برنامج التغذية التكميلية المستهدفة سجل قبول 445,230 طفلاً تتراوح أعمارهم بين 6 و59 شهراً، بما يعادل 42.4% من المستهدف، إلى جانب 153,721 امرأة حامل ومرضع، بنسبة تغطية بلغت 60.9%. وبيّن أن نتائج برنامج التغذية التكميلية الشاملة ظلت متدنية للغاية، حيث لم تتجاوز نسبة تحقيق المستهدف 2.6% للأطفال دون الخامسة و3% للنساء الحوامل والمرضعات. وتحدث التقرير عن تقديم الشركاء مكملات فيتامين «أ» إلى 4,453,397 طفلاً تتراوح أعمارهم بين 6 و59 شهراً، في 131 محلية، كما قدموا مكملات الحديد وحمض الفوليك إلى 982,746 امرأة حامل ومرضع في 154 محلية. تحذيرات جديدة وتوقع التقرير استمرار تدهور الوضع التغذوي خلال الربع الرابع من العام، نظراً إلى ارتفاع حالات القبول في برامج التغذية العلاجية والتكميلية، إضافة إلى زيادة معدلات سوء التغذية التي كشفت عنها المسوحات، خصوصاً في ولايات دارفور. وربط هذه التوقعات أيضاً بتدهور الأمن الغذائي والبدء المبكر لموسم الجوع في عام 2027، مرجحاً استمرار ارتفاع حالات القبول في برامج التغذية العلاجية والتكميلية، خلافاً للاتجاه التنازلي الذي سُجل في سنوات سابقة. وفي السنوات السابقة، كانت فترة حصاد المحاصيل الممتدة من أكتوبر إلى بداية العام تشهد توافراً في الغذاء مع انخفاض أسعاره، لكن الجفاف المرتبط بظاهرة النينيو غطى مساحات شاسعة من الأراضي الزراعية. الكلمات: أزمة التغذية الأمم المتحدة الخرطوم السودان اليونيسف دارفور سوء التغذية في السودان Their security is consequently inseparable from the stability of the Horn of Africa, the institutional capacity of neighbouring states and the resilience of international supply chains. Disruptions to commercial navigation, whether arising from armed attacks, piracy, geopolitical confrontation or institutional fragility, generate consequences that extend far beyond the immediate theatre of instability. Within this strategic environment, attempts to conceptualise Red Sea governance as the exclusive preserve of a select group of littoral states risk confusing territorial jurisdiction with the broader responsibilities of maritime security. Coastal states possess sovereign rights and jurisdiction recognised under international law; those rights must be respected. Yet sovereignty over territorial waters does not translate into an exclusive entitlement to determine the entire security architecture of a maritime corridor whose stability affects landlocked economies, international shipping and distant trading partners alike. Ethiopia’s case rests on precisely this distinction. Its geographical position, demographic scale, economic significance and dependence on maritime transit establish compelling grounds for substantive participation in regional deliberations concerning navigation, commercial resilience and maritime-security cooperation. Excluding Ethiopia from such arrangements would disregard the interconnected character of contemporary security, in which the vulnerabilities of one state can rapidly become the liabilities of an entire region. An effective Red Sea security order must therefore move beyond narrow geographical formalism towards a model of differentiated but shared responsibility. Littoral states would retain their sovereign prerogatives, while landlocked countries and other materially affected partners would contribute according to their capabilities, interests and agreed institutional mandates. Such an approach would neither diminish coastal sovereignty nor confer unilateral privileges upon Ethiopia. Rather, it would align the distribution of security responsibilities with the realities of regional interdependence. International Law and the Rights of Landlocked States International law provides an important foundation for this approach, although its provisions must be interpreted with precision. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) recognises the right of landlocked states to access to and from the sea for the purpose of exercising the rights conferred by the Convention. Part X further provides for freedom of transit through the territories of transit states, subject to mutually agreed terms and modalities. These provisions establish a legal basis for negotiated maritime access and transit arrangements; they do not, however, confer automatic rights to territorial sovereignty, a coastline or a naval presence in another state’s waters. The distinction is consequential. Ethiopia’s geographical circumstances do not extinguish its legitimate maritime interests, but the realisation of those interests must proceed through negotiated agreements, reciprocal commitments and respect for the sovereignty of coastal neighbours. Its objective should therefore be the institutionalisation of dependable access and meaningful participation in cooperative maritime security, rather than the assertion of unilateral legal entitlements unsupported by international law. UNCLOS also recognises the importance of cooperation in the management of semi-enclosed seas. Article 123 calls upon states bordering such seas to coordinate their activities and, where appropriate, to cooperate with other interested states and international organisations in matters including resource management, environmental protection and scientific research. Although this provision does not establish an unrestricted right to participate in every aspect of maritime governance, it reinforces the broader principle that the management of interconnected marine environments benefits from structured cooperation. For Ethiopia, these legal principles offer a constructive basis for diplomacy. Its substantial reliance on Red Sea trade gives it a compelling interest in the security of maritime approaches, the predictability of transit arrangements and the continuity of commercial navigation. The appropriate response is to translate that interest into durable bilateral and multilateral frameworks that recognise the rights of coastal states while ensuring that Ethiopia’s economic and security concerns receive institutional consideration. The governing principle should be straightforward: coastal sovereignty and the legitimate interests of landlocked states are not mutually exclusive; they must be reconciled through law, negotiation and reciprocal benefit. Precedents for Mutually Beneficial Maritime Access International practice demonstrates that geographical constraints need not condemn landlocked states to permanent logistical vulnerability. Across regions, governments have employed bilateral agreements, dedicated port facilities, transport corridors, customs arrangements and long-term commercial concessions to establish more predictable access to maritime trade. The 1965 boundary agreement between Jordan and Saudi Arabia, for example, reconfigured territory in the Gulf of Aqaba region and expanded Jordan’s coastline. Although rooted in a particular historical and territorial context, the agreement illustrates how negotiated settlements can reshape geographical constraints where the parties identify compatible strategic interests. It should not be treated as a template readily transferable to the Horn of Africa, but it demonstrates the possibilities and limitations of diplomacy in addressing questions of territorial access. A more directly applicable model lies in the development of transport and port corridors linking landlocked economies to coastal infrastructure. Arrangements associated with the Port of Nacala and Malawi illustrate how dedicated terminal capacity, improved rail and road connections, streamlined border procedures and coordinated logistics can generate reciprocal economic benefits. The coastal state gains transit revenue, investment and employment, while the landlocked partner obtains more reliable access to international markets. Comparable mechanisms could form the foundation of a more durable Ethiopia–coastal state partnership. Long-term port-utilisation agreements, dedicated terminal concessions, bonded logistics facilities, preferential commercial arrangements and integrated transport corridors could reduce Ethiopia’s exposure to logistical disruption while generating tangible economic returns for host countries. Where mutually acceptable, such agreements could incorporate joint investment, infrastructure development and coordinated security protocols. The essential consideration is reciprocity. Maritime access must not be framed as a zero-sum contest between Ethiopia and its coastal neighbours. Properly designed agreements can transform geographical proximity into a source of shared prosperity, giving coastal states a material interest in Ethiopia’s economic success while reducing the vulnerabilities associated with uncertain or excessively concentrated transit arrangements. Such arrangements would also provide a practical foundation for a more structured Ethiopian contribution to regional maritime security. Participation could include information-sharing, logistical assistance, coordinated threat assessments, capacity-building and other forms of cooperation negotiated with the relevant coastal authorities. Any naval deployment or operational presence would require an appropriate legal basis and the consent of the state concerned. These safeguards are not impediments to cooperation; they are the conditions that make it legitimate and sustainable. Historical Experience and Ethiopia’s Maritime Reorientation Ethiopia’s contemporary maritime predicament must also be understood in its historical context. Before Eritrea’s independence in 1993, Ethiopia possessed a coastline of approximately 700 kilometres and maintained a naval force with facilities associated with Massawa, Assab and the Dahlak Islands. Its maritime institutions formed part of a broader national security structure, connecting coastal defence, naval training and the protection of strategic approaches. The loss of direct access to the sea fundamentally altered Ethiopia’s strategic environment, but it did not eliminate the country’s dependence on maritime commerce. Nor did it diminish the regional consequences of instability along the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The resulting asymmetry between Ethiopia’s continental economic significance and its dependence on infrastructure located beyond its sovereign territory remains a central feature of the country’s strategic calculations. Historical experience, however, should inform contemporary policy without dictating it. The restoration of Ethiopia’s maritime role cannot simply replicate the institutional arrangements of an earlier era, nor can historical possession of a coastline constitute a contemporary legal claim to territory belonging to another sovereign state. The circumstances of the region have changed, as have the legal and diplomatic conditions under which maritime cooperation must now operate. What remains relevant is the strategic lesson: a state whose prosperity depends heavily on maritime access has a compelling interest in the stability, predictability and security of the systems through which that access is exercised. Ethiopia’s long-term objective should therefore be to develop the economic, diplomatic and institutional capabilities necessary to protect its maritime interests through mutually agreed arrangements. The deterioration of security across parts of the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden makes this objective increasingly consequential. Threats to commercial shipping, attacks by armed non-state actors and the strategic competition surrounding vital maritime chokepoints expose the limitations of fragmented security responses. No single coastal administration, particularly one operating under substantial institutional and resource constraints, can be expected to neutralise every threat to a corridor of such international importance. Nevertheless, Ethiopia’s demographic and economic scale should not be mistaken for an automatic capacity to provide maritime security. Effective naval operations require specialised personnel, sustained financing, maritime surveillance, logistics, training, command structures and operational experience. A credible Ethiopian contribution would therefore require a carefully sequenced programme of institutional development, supported by diplomatic cooperation and realistic assessments of national resources. The strategic objective is not to substitute Ethiopian predominance for coastal-state authority. It is to ensure that Ethiopia’s substantial stake in the corridor is matched by an appropriate, lawful and operationally credible contribution to its security. Regional Security Contributions and Maritime Responsibility / Ethiopia’s record of involvement in regional security provides a relevant foundation for this endeavour. Its participation in African Union missions in Somalia, including sustained operations against Al-Shabaab, has demonstrated the extent to which its national security is intertwined with the stability of neighbouring states. Ethiopian diplomacy has also contributed to regional mediation efforts, including the 1972 Addis Ababa Agreement that ended the first Sudanese civil war and diplomatic engagement surrounding Sudan’s political transition in 2019. These experiences do not automatically establish a claim to maritime authority. They do, however, demonstrate that Ethiopia has substantial experience in security cooperation and a direct interest in preventing instability from spreading across the Horn of Africa. Extending that experience to maritime-security initiatives would be a logical development, provided it is guided by clear mandates, institutional preparedness and the consent of relevant partners. A modern Ethiopian maritime strategy should consequently integrate several mutually reinforcing priorities: dependable commercial access, diversified transit arrangements, maritime-domain awareness, cooperation against transnational threats and the development of specialised naval capabilities where economically and strategically justified. These objectives should be pursued incrementally, with an emphasis on professional competence, regional confidence-building and transparent legal arrangements. The wider Horn of Africa would benefit from an approach that treats maritime security as a shared regional public good rather than an instrument of geopolitical exclusion. Coastal states would retain control over their sovereign waters, while Ethiopia could contribute resources, expertise and institutional capacity to cooperative initiatives serving the interests of all participants. Such a framework would also reduce the risk that maritime access becomes a recurring source of bilateral tension. By embedding cooperation within durable agreements, the parties could replace episodic political bargaining with predictable mechanisms for resolving disputes, financing infrastructure and responding to emerging threats. The Strategic Case for International Engagement For international partners whose commercial prosperity depends on uninterrupted navigation through the Bab el-Mandeb and the southern Red Sea, an inclusive regional security architecture is a matter of practical strategic interest. The deployment of distant naval forces can provide important protection against immediate threats, but external intervention alone cannot substitute indefinitely for capable regional institutions, resilient transport networks and sustained political cooperation among neighbouring states. Ethiopia could become a more consequential contributor to this architecture, particularly through its diplomatic influence, economic weight and experience in regional security operations. Its participation would be most effective if embedded in a broader framework involving coastal governments, regional organisations and international partners, with clearly defined responsibilities and respect for the sovereignty of every participating state. International support should therefore prioritise the conditions that make cooperation viable: infrastructure investment, technical assistance, professional training, maritime information-sharing and the strengthening of regional mechanisms for crisis prevention. Any support for the development of Ethiopian naval capabilities should be assessed against clear objectives, available resources and the need to build confidence among neighbouring countries. The purpose of such engagement would not be to establish an Ethiopian sphere of influence over the Red Sea. It would be to create a more balanced distribution of responsibility for protecting a maritime corridor whose security is indispensable to regional development and global commerce. An Ethiopia that enjoys predictable maritime access, maintains constructive relations with coastal neighbours and contributes proportionately to regional security would offer international partners a more sustainable basis for cooperation than a regional order characterised by mistrust, fragmented responsibilities and recurring disputes over access. From Strategic Interest to a Durable Regional Order Ambassador Redwan Hussein’s remarks at the Tana High-Level Forum point towards a fundamental proposition: the security of the Red Sea must be organised around the realities of interdependence rather than the restrictive logic of geographical exclusion. The corridor’s importance to global commerce, coupled with the interconnected vulnerabilities of the Horn of Africa, makes inclusive cooperation a strategic necessity rather than a diplomatic courtesy. For Ethiopia, the implications are clear. Its maritime interests must be pursued through international law, negotiated access arrangements, sustained investment in national capabilities and a foreign policy that treats coastal neighbours as indispensable partners rather than obstacles to be overcome. For littoral states, a more engaged Ethiopia offers opportunities for infrastructure development, expanded trade, shared security initiatives and a broader distribution of the responsibilities associated with regional stability. The international community, meanwhile, has an interest in supporting arrangements that are both operationally effective and politically legitimate. A maritime security order that excludes a major regional economy risks leaving important vulnerabilities unaddressed; one that disregards coastal sovereignty would generate new sources of instability. The challenge is to construct an institutional framework capable of avoiding both extremes. Ultimately, the future of Red Sea security will depend less on assertions of exclusive entitlement than on the ability of regional states to reconcile legitimate national interests within a common strategic framework. Ethiopia’s case is strongest when grounded in that principle: not a demand for privileges beyond international law, but a compelling argument for meaningful participation commensurate with its economic exposure, regional responsibilities and capacity to contribute. The Red Sea is too strategically consequential to be governed through exclusion, and its security too interdependent to be sustained by fragmented responsibility. An inclusive, legally grounded and mutually beneficial maritime order one that respects coastal sovereignty while recognising the legitimate interests of landlocked states is therefore not merely desirable. It is essential to the long-term stability of the Horn of Africa and the uninterrupted functioning of one of the global economy’s most critical maritime arteries. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia’s Maritime Diplomacy in a Contested Red Sea – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-11-02 Ethiopia’s Maritime Diplomacy in a Contested Red Sea 0 Comments On October 26, 2026, Addis Ababa hosted a gathering that would ordinarily be expected to take place in a coastal capital. Naval commanders and maritime representatives from Yemen, Oman, Djibouti, Somaliland and Puntland joined the Ethiopian Navy for a four day workshop on maritime search and rescue, information sharing and regional security. The meeting, which concludes on October 29, brought together authorities connected to some of the most strategically important coastlines in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. According to coverage of the Ethiopian National Defense Force announcement , the discussions aimed to strengthen coordination and improve responses to maritime emergencies. Beyond these immediate objectives, however, the gathering offers an opportunity to examine Ethiopia’s growing engagement with a region from which its geography has long separated it. Since Eritrea’s secession in 1993, Ethiopia has relied on neighboring countries for maritime access. This dependence carries considerable economic consequences. According to the World Bank , Djibouti handled approximately 95 percent of Ethiopian imports and exports at the time of its assessment, demonstrating the importance of a single corridor to the country’s external trade. Diversification through Berbera and other regional ports has therefore become increasingly important. Yet access to port infrastructure addresses only part of Ethiopia’s maritime concerns. The security of shipping routes, the reliability of regional partners and the institutions responsible for managing maritime emergencies also affect the country’s economic interests. The Addis Ababa meeting becomes particularly interesting when placed against the competing diplomatic arrangements emerging around the Red Sea. In January 2020, eight countries established the Council of Arab and African States Bordering the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden . Its members include Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan, Somalia, Djibouti, Yemen and Jordan. Membership was organized around coastal geography, leaving Ethiopia outside a forum concerned with the security of waters through which much of its international trade passes. This exclusion has acquired greater political significance as regional countries develop closer security relationships. On October 4, 2026, the leaders of Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan met in New Alamein and adopted a joint declaration affirming that Red Sea governance should remain the exclusive responsibility of littoral states. The declaration also rejected recognition of Somaliland and addressed disagreements concerning the Nile. These positions reveal an approach to regional governance that places significant emphasis on coastal sovereignty and territorial integrity. For Ethiopia, the challenge is clear. Its economic and security interests are tied to the Red Sea, yet some of the emerging regional arrangements provide no formal place for a landlocked country. The Addis Ababa workshop does not overturn these restrictions, nor does it establish a competing maritime alliance. It does, however, demonstrate that Ethiopia can engage coastal authorities through other forms of cooperation. Maritime governance is not confined to political councils; information sharing, emergency response and professional coordination also provide opportunities for meaningful participation. The composition of the gathering is particularly relevant in this respect. Djibouti remains Ethiopia’s principal gateway to international markets, making cooperation between the two countries essential to regional commerce. Somaliland, meanwhile, has become important to Ethiopia’s efforts to diversify its transport corridors through the development of Berbera port and its associated infrastructure . Puntland’s geographical position along the Gulf of Aden gives it an important role in maritime affairs near the approaches to the Indian Ocean. Their participation demonstrates that Ethiopia already maintains channels of communication with authorities responsible for maritime areas directly connected to its commercial interests. These relationships should not be mistaken for unconditional political support. Somaliland’s unresolved international status and Puntland’s disagreements with Somalia’s federal government introduce complications that cannot be ignored. In March 2024, Puntland announced that it would no longer recognize the authority of Somalia’s federal institutions following disputed constitutional amendments. Ethiopia’s own relations with Mogadishu were strained by the January 2024 memorandum of understanding with Somaliland, before the Ankara Declaration of December 2024 established a framework for pursuing mutually beneficial maritime arrangements while respecting Somalia’s sovereignty. Somalia’s federal government was notably absent from the list of participants, although it remains unclear whether Mogadishu was invited. Still, Ethiopia’s engagement with Somaliland and Puntland does not necessarily have to come at the expense of its relations with Somalia. Addis Ababa has an interest in maintaining ties with all three, particularly given their importance to security along the Gulf of Aden. The challenge will be to strengthen these relationships without deepening existing political disagreements. The participation of Yemen and Oman extends the meeting’s relevance beyond the Horn of Africa. Yemen occupies a critical position near Bab al Mandeb, where instability can disrupt shipping between the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea. However, Yemen’s internal fragmentation limits what cooperation with its internationally recognized authorities can accomplish. As a 2026 British parliamentary assessment explains, the Houthi movement controls much of northwestern Yemen and has expanded its influence along parts of the Red Sea coastline. Oman brings a different perspective through its position along the Arabian Peninsula and its connections to the wider Indian Ocean. For Ethiopia, engagement with these authorities offers opportunities for communication, maritime safety cooperation and professional exchanges. It does not guarantee their support for Ethiopian naval basing or sea access negotiations. Nevertheless, regular contact can help build the confidence required for more substantial agreements. Relationships established around less contentious matters may eventually support discussions on broader economic and security interests. The meeting also forms part of an established international framework rather than an exclusively Ethiopian initiative. As reports on the workshop indicate, the event is associated with the European Union supported Crisis Response Project for the Red Sea and Western Indian Ocean, alongside CRIMARIO and Expertise France. These initiatives emphasize maritime awareness, information sharing and improved coordination. Ethiopia’s contribution lies in hosting regional representatives and participating in a wider system of cooperation supported by international partners. Importantly, Ethiopia’s involvement in maritime security predates the current meeting. The country was among the original signatories of the Djibouti Code of Conduct in 2009 , which established a framework for cooperation against piracy and armed robbery at sea. More recently, an International Maritime Organization workshop held in Addis Ababa in August 2026 produced a roadmap for establishing a National Maritime Information Sharing Centre. The proposed institution would improve coordination among Ethiopian agencies and strengthen their connections to regional maritime information networks. This is perhaps the clearest evidence of practical progress. A functioning information sharing centre could help Ethiopia monitor developments affecting its commercial interests, coordinate responses to maritime incidents and maintain contact with regional partners. Such capabilities would not resolve the logistical difficulties of operating a navy without a sovereign coastline. Naval deployment still requires access to suitable ports, maintenance facilities and operational infrastructure. Nevertheless, institutional capacity and diplomatic relationships are necessary components of any credible maritime strategy. Ethiopia’s interest in the Red Sea should therefore be understood through both its ambitions and its existing opportunities. The country has legitimate economic reasons to seek dependable maritime access, while neighboring states have their own sovereignty and security concerns. Cooperation offers a means of pursuing these interests without treating them as necessarily incompatible. Ethiopia’s commercial demand, transport infrastructure and regional relationships can provide incentives for arrangements that also benefit coastal partners. For Ethiopia, this is an encouraging beginning. Its maritime future cannot rest solely on negotiations over a particular port or coastline. It will also be shaped by the relationships it builds with neighboring countries and its contribution to the security of the region. The lasting impact of the October gathering remains to be seen, but its immediate significance should not be dismissed. In a region where competing political interests often dominate discussions of the Red Sea, cooperation offers Ethiopia an additional path through which to advance its economic interests, strengthen diplomatic relationships and establish a more enduring role in regional maritime affairs. ethiopia.content: Sudan complains to UN Security Council over drone attacks from Ethiopia | Kuwait Times Newspaper Home Kuwait World Middle East Subcontinent Asia Africa America Europe Opinion Your Take Conspiracy Theory Editor's Desk Others Business Sports Football Cricket Shooting Tennis Other Sports Lifestyle Movies & Music Art & Fashion Food Archive PDF Merch World OMDURMAN, Sudan: Journalists document damage at the Al-Markhiyat power station north of Omdurman on October 28, 2026, after a reported drone strike by Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. — AFP Sudan complains to UN Security Council over drone attacks from Ethiopia Khartoum says 187 drones launched from Ethiopian territory this year; Addis Ababa denies involvement November 02, 2026 01:42 p.m Share Share Options Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter Telegram LinkedIn Whatsapp KHARTOUM: Sudan has filed complaints against Ethiopia with the UN Security Council and the African Union, accusing Addis Ababa of allowing the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to launch drone strikes on civilian facilities from its territory. Sudan’s military, which has been fighting the RSF since April 2023, has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of aiding the paramilitary group, including by allowing drone attacks from Ethiopian territory. Ethiopia denies the accusations and has in turn accused the Sudanese army of backing rebels linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which Khartoum rejects. In a statement on Sunday, Sudan’s army-aligned foreign ministry accused Ethiopia of “blatant aggression” in its formal complaints to the Security Council and the AU Peace and Security Council. “The use of Ethiopian territory by the terrorist militia (RSF) to target Sudanese territory is considered a hostile act that places Ethiopia in violation of international law,” it said. In a report on Sunday, Sudan’s army-led Transitional Sovereignty Council said it had documented 70 attacks this year involving 187 one-way attack drones launched from Ethiopian territory, killing or wounding nearly 500 civilians. It said the attacks targeted residential complexes, hospitals and power and fuel stations. Both the army and the RSF have increasingly relied on drones that can strike targets hundreds of kilometers away without putting their fighters at risk. ethiopia.content: As Eritrea Continues to Orchestrate Attacks from Its Territory, Ethiopia Retains Its Inherent Right to Self-Defence – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-11-02 As Eritrea Continues to Orchestrate Attacks from Its Territory, Ethiopia Retains Its Inherent Right to Self-Defence 0 Comments Ethiopia’s security concerns with Eritrea extend well beyond the presence of Eritrean troops inside its internationally recognised territory. Of equal, if not greater, concern is Eritrea’s provision of political, military and logistical support to Ethiopian armed opposition groups, enabling them to coordinate their activities and pursue armed attacks against the Ethiopian state and the constitutional order thereof, from Eritrean territory. The challenge for Addis Ababa is therefore not simply to secure its borders, but to address the external infrastructure sustaining armed threats against the state, without being drawn into another interstate war. Avoiding such a confrontation, however, cannot mean accepting an indefinite deterioration of Ethiopia’s security environment. As discussed in Horn Review’s recent analyses, Eritrea’s Incursion and Ethiopia’s Right to Self-Defence: Where Does the Law Stand? and Ethiopia’s Right to Self-Defence and the Strategic Fallacy of Symmetrical De-escalation , Eritrea’s military involvement inside Ethiopia and its longstanding relationships with armed opposition movements must be understood as interconnected security concerns. The formation of the seven-group Coalition of Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival in September 2026 brings this relationship into sharper focus. The alliance brings together organisations with fundamentally different political orientations, ethnic constituencies and histories of armed confrontation. Their common opposition to the federal government does not translate into a coherent political programme or a shared vision for Ethiopia’s future. The inclusion of the TPLF is particularly revealing. During the TPLF-dominated EPRDF era, Eritrea supported armed movements fighting against the Ethiopian government, including organisations now associated with the new coalition. The TPLF, once the dominant force in the government these movements opposed, has now joined them against the federal government. This extraordinary reversal suggests that the coalition’s immediate cohesion rests less on ideological reconciliation than on a common adversary and the external patronage attributed to Asmara. Recently leaked intelligence reports provide a more immediate indication of this emerging alignment. According to the reports, Jaal Mero of the Oromo Liberation Army, Zemene Kassie of Amhara Fano and Debretsion Gebremichael of the TPLF held a convention in Asmara despite repeated diplomatic warnings from Addis Ababa. The press release issued on 31 October 2026 reportedly followed that meeting. The same information suggests that the Eritrean regime and elements within the Sudanese Armed Forces are encouraging the groups to intensify their military campaigns against Ethiopia, with assurances of continued political, logistical and other assistance. The significance of the Asmara meeting lies in its apparent effort to revive an Eritrean military strategy that had already failed on the battlefield. In its late September 2026 iteration, the plan sought to bring the fight against the Ethiopian state into its own territory, using insurgent groups organised into a seven-group coalition as the ground force. The coalition was assembled and officiated roughly two weeks before Eritrea launched its offensive on the northern Tigray and north-eastern Afar fronts. That campaign was subsequently pushed back by the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF), which advanced on both fronts, regained control of Ethiopian territory and forced much of the TPLF and Eritrean troops to retreat. Fighters belonging to the coalition were also pushed back. The reported gathering in Asmara therefore points to an attempt to reconstitute this failed strategy: coordinating and supporting armed groups from within Eritrean territory to continue the war campaign against Ethiopia, rather than abandoning the objective after the initial offensive was defeated. Ethiopian national wealth, including gold, is also being transported into Eritrea in connection with armed networks operating against Ethiopia, adding a further economic dimension to the problem. These developments, once again, coincide with Ethiopia’s repeated accusations of Eritrean military incursions and material support for insurgent groups operating inside the country. Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos has repeatedly demanded the withdrawal of Eritrean forces and an end to their collaboration with armed opposition groups over the past two years. Despite repeated diplomatic representations, including after Eritrea severed diplomatic ties with Ethiopia, Addis Ababa maintains that the violations have continued. The matter reached the United Nations Security Council in early October 2026. In a letter submitted on 9 October, Ethiopia accused Eritrean forces, including mechanised units, of advancing as far as 60 kilometres into northern Ethiopian territory. At this point, Eritrea’s unceasing aggressive military posturing, its compartmentalised provocations and overt violations, its provision of military and logistical assistance and the Eritrean military incursions point to a security challenge that cannot be addressed through diplomatic procedures alone. Ethiopia has repeatedly communicated its concerns and sought international engagement. But diplomacy cannot become an indefinite substitute for the protection of national security, particularly when the conduct at issue continues despite repeated warnings. Ethiopia thus retains its inherent right to self-defense, something that has remained intact since Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia’s territory in what the later considers an act of war. Article 51 of the United Nations Charter preserves the inherent right of individual and collective self-defence in the event of an armed attack. Where a state is directly involved in such an attack, or armed groups operating from its territory carry out attacks meeting the applicable threshold under international law, the victim state retains its right to defend itself. The existence of an international border does not, by itself, extinguish that entitlement. Nor should Ethiopia be expected to wait until another offensive has been launched from Eritrean territory, its forces have crossed the border en masse again and its population has suffered the consequences. While the scope of anticipatory self-defence remains contested under international law, Ethiopia or any state for that matter is not required to disregard a demonstrable and sufficiently imminent threat from a hostile regime right across its borders. It must retain the capacity to protect its territory and population through measures consistent with international law. The danger of another interstate war is real, but it cannot become a permanent constraint on Ethiopia’s ability to respond to external threats. Eritrea can not and should not be allowed to continue to provide sanctuary and support to armed organisations operating against Ethiopia, and orchestrate attack from its territory into Ethiopia, while Addis Ababa is expected to confine itself to diplomatic procedures for fear of escalation. Such an arrangement would place the entire burden of restraint on the state whose security is being persistently challenged and whose sovereignty has been repeatedly violated. Ethiopia must therefore maintain diplomatic pressure while preserving a credible capacity for self-defence. This requires continued monitoring and documentation of Eritrean military activities, international engagement, stronger border security, the disruption of financial and logistical networks sustaining armed operations and, when necessary, to use force to defend it-self and its key national security interests that are being put at imminent risk by the Eritrean regime. The objective is not to widen the confrontation, but to ensure that Ethiopia’s commitment to peaceful coexistence is not mistaken for an inability or unwillingness to defend itself. Ethiopia does not have to choose between pursuing pragmatic diplomacy and defending itself. It has every reason to avoid another war with Eritrea, but no obligation to tolerate an increasingly hostile security environment simply to prevent one. Its diplomatic restraint must remain a sovereign choice, not a vulnerability that another state can exploit indefinitely. Ethiopia retains its inherent right to take the measures necessary and lawful to defend its territory, population and constitutional order. The avoidance of war must never become an obligation to wait for another round of aggression from Eritrea. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia and the Red Sea: A Civilizational Case for Maritime Access. Perspectives from the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa - IFA Contact Us English Subscribe Topics Regions Events Publications Academy Media About Us ← Back to Blog Policy Briefs • 12 min read • November 2, 2026 Ethiopia and the Red Sea: A Civilizational Case for Maritime Access. Perspectives from the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa Ethiopia and the Red Sea: A Civilizational Case for Maritime Access. Perspectives from the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa Executive Summary With more than 130 million people, Ethiopia is the most populous landlocked country in the world. On 24 October 2026, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed told the Tana High-Level Forum in Bahir Dar that sea access is an existential matter for such a nation. This brief explains why Addis Ababa holds that view and why the position is reasonable. The argument runs on three levels: geography, access, and strategy. The brief also reads the Forum's discussion of Red Sea security as the most practical route to a negotiated settlement that serves Ethiopia and its neighbors alike. 1. The anomaly Among its historical peers, Ethiopia is the only large state without a coast. Turkey, Iran, India, China, and Italy all descend from old empires, and each is smaller today than its predecessors. None has lost its connection to the water; each is still defined in part by a strait, a gulf, an ocean front, or a sea. Ethiopia fits the first half of this pattern: an ancient civilization that contracted into a modern state and endured. It departs from the pattern in the second half because among these peers it alone has no coast. The comparison does not suggest that these histories are identical. It shows that a lasting maritime connection is the norm, not the exception, for states of Ethiopia's age and scale. The policy question is how the gap came about and whether it must remain. 2. Civilization with a maritime past Aksum, the ancestral kingdom of modern Ethiopia, took shape around the first century CE and prospered from its position between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. Its port at Adulis attracted traders from Egypt, Greece, Rome, and Arabia, and by the sixth century Aksum's authority extended across the water to southern Arabia. Ancient sources describe Adulis as part of a trade network that linked the Mediterranean to the Indian Ocean in the middle of the first century. Ethiopia's interest in the Red Sea today therefore revives a thread that runs back to the earliest years of its statehood. The historical record explains the depth of this interest. It does not by itself settle how access should be arranged, which is a matter for negotiation. 3. The Retreat to the Highlands Aksum declined after Rome fell and the trade that sustained it dried up. [2] The center of gravity moved south and inland, into highlands that protected Ethiopia's independence for centuries. The same terrain drew later with political capitals, Lalibela and Gondar among them, away from the coast. Ethiopia did not turn away from the sea. Shifting regional balances and the pressure of rival powers made the highlands the safest base, and the mountains became a refuge. 4. The Tana Forum and the Medemer Position The 12th Tana Forum was held in Bahir Dar from 23 to 25 October under the theme 'Pathways to Peace in Africa: Economic Sovereignty and Geopolitical Transformation. [4] Prime Minister Abiy spoke at the opening alongside Ghana's President John Mahama, who chairs the Forum this year, and African Union Chairperson Evariste Ndayishimiye. In his address at the opening session, Prime Minister Abiy argued that planning for future generations is difficult when every route to world markets crosses another country's territory. For a country of more than 130 million, he said, access to the sea is existential, and Ethiopia will continue to pursue it through dialogue and mutual benefit. [1] The report of the speech linked the dependence on foreign ports to sovereignty, security, and trade competitiveness and placed the point within a wider African debate on economic independence. The day before, at the Forum's Special Envoy Dialogue, Ambassador Redwan Hussen said that no small group of states can guarantee the security of the Red Sea alone. He cited growing militarization, rivalry between outside powers, and renewed attacks on merchant shipping and noted that Ethiopia's maritime trade is entirely dependent on that sea. [7] The Forum does not negotiate binding agreements, but its value lies in how it frames the issue. That two senior Ethiopian officials raised the matter on a high-level African diplomacy and security platform shows the priority the government attaches to it. These remarks continued a line set out on 5 October, when Abiy took the oath for a second term at the opening of the seventh parliament and the Prime Minister's Office named the new administration the 'Medemer Government.' [8] In his address, he said that Ethiopian civilization cannot be fully realized without a port of entry and exit. [9] In his statements, the prime minister has emphasized a diplomatic approach based on give and take rather than the use of force. [10] The message has been consistent: History explains why the matter counts, economics explains why it is urgent, and dialogue is the method. Two features of this structure deserve attention. First, Ethiopia ties its claim to a shared regional interest in the stability of the Red Sea, which broadens its audience beyond its immediate neighbors. Second, by committing publicly to dialogue and mutual benefit, it sets a standard against which its own conduct can be judged and which its partners can be asked to match. 5. Three Levels of Argument The first level is geography. The heartlands of Turkey, Iran, India, China, and Italy sit on coasts, rivers, and straits. Ethiopia's heartland drifted inland over the centuries, the result of history rather than national preference. The second is access. The states with which Ethiopia shares an ancient statehood and civilizational ties kept or adapted their maritime reach as empires gave way to modern borders. Ethiopia, through a different and complex historical trajectory, was unable to do so. It lost direct access to the Red Sea in 1993, when Eritrea became independent. [11] Few large historical states have had to manage a gap of this kind. The third is strategy. Turkey makes use of its straits and Iran of its gulf coast. Ethiopia routes most of its trade through neighboring states, especially Djibouti, and depends on their ports. Unlike most of its historical peers, it lacks the strategic advantages that sea access providers to the protection and promotion of national power. This structural dependence is the limitation the Medemer Government seeks to address. The three levels reinforce each other. Geography explains how the gap arose, access explains why it persists, and strategy explains why it matters now. Reliance on a small number of corridors also concentrates risk, since a disruption at one port or along one route affects the whole economy. Reliable and diversified access is therefore the underlying objective. 6. Conclusions Ethiopia's case is best put as a plea for fairness. A civilization of more than two thousand years and more than 130 million people should not have to depend on others for its door to the world. The Medemer Government can make this case more effectively by pairing its historical foundation with concrete reciprocity, meaning tangible benefits offered to partners in return, and by showing that Ethiopian access would add to the stability of the Red Sea. Keeping the discussion anchored in respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of every state in the region will also strengthen Ethiopia's credibility with the African Union and its international partners. 7. Policy recommendations The following steps aim to turn the Tana messaging into a sustained and practical diplomatic effort. • Maintain momentum. Keep communicating Ethiopia's concerns to regional bodies and the international community in comparable forums, with consistent messaging, until the required goals are met. • Use the Tana frame as a bridge. The call for shared Red Sea security gives Ethiopia common ground with coastal states. Bring it to the African Union, IGAD, and bilateral talks and propose a structured consultation on Red Sea security and maritime access that is open to both coastal and noncoastal states. • Pair the historical case with reciprocity. Prepare a set of mutually beneficial options, such as commercial, infrastructure, and security cooperation, which can be presented to partners in bilateral discussions. • In the meantime, strengthen existing corridors. Deepen the arrangements with current port partners so that trade becomes more dependable and less exposed to disruption while longer-term discussions continue. • Build an evidence base. Commission a short, data-led study on the economic cost of dependence and the available options, for use in diplomatic briefings and public communication. • Keep diplomatic language consistent. Emphasize dialogue, mutual benefit, and respect for sovereignty and international law in every public statement, so that the position is received as a cooperative proposal. Notes 1. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked country, emphasizes the critical need for maritime access to the Red Sea, as articulated by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed at the 12th Tana High-Level Forum. He argues that access to the sea is essential for Ethiopia's economic sovereignty and security, especially given its historical maritime connections dating back to the Aksumite Empire. The forum highlighted Ethiopia's unique position among large historical states that maintain coastal access, underscoring the strategic disadvantages it faces since losing direct access to the Red Sea in 1993. Abiy's government seeks to address this gap through dialogue and mutual benefit, advocating for a collaborative approach to Red Sea security that includes both coastal and non-coastal states. The Tana Forum serves as a platform for Ethiopia to articulate its maritime aspirations while promoting regional stability and cooperation. The government aims to strengthen existing trade routes and engage in diplomatic efforts to secure reliable access to the sea. (160 words)

ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy's Medemer Govt Senior Leadership Taking 'Military Training'at Hurso Center - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy's Medemer Govt Senior Leadership Taking 'Military Training'at Hurso Center Addis Standard PM Abiy said that military science and experience could help cultivate the “discipline, accountability, coordination, and sense of patriotism” expected of government leaders. 31 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Senior leaders of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's Medemer Government are undergoing military training at the Hurso Military Training Center, according to PM Abiy, who said the exercise as part of efforts to strengthen leadership capacity, discipline, national security, and the implementation of its broader development vision. In a statement outlining the rationale for the training, Abiy said the Medemer Government's ambition to "build Ethiopia's civilization" based on comprehensive prosperity required leaders who were physically developed, morally strong, intellectually prepared, and mature in wisdom. "Leadership requires comprehensive preparedness," Abiy said, describing comprehensive prosperity as encompassing material and spiritual well-being alongside cultural and moral development. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He argued that military science and experience could help cultivate the "discipline, accountability, coordination, and sense of patriotism" expected of government leaders. According to Abiy, the training is intended to equip senior officials with skills and experience that can be applied to implementing the government's Medemer vision, including aligning strategic thinking, mobilizing public participation, fulfilling commitments to citizens, and strengthening national security. The prime minister said military training could also help leaders improve coordination across government structures, from the grassroots to the national level, while fostering a sense of responsibility for the country's future. "Military science, experience, and life are unrivaled in shaping human purpose and personality," Abiy said, arguing that military institutions instill physical and moral discipline, work ethic, teamwork, and readiness to carry out assigned responsibilities. He further linked the exercise to the government's ambition to build what he described as an "unshakeable country" capable of resisting internal and external challenges, while preparing succeeding generations for leadership. "Soldiers have targets; civilians have a purpose. The goal of both is to achieve victory," Abiy said. "By harmonizing both disciplines, we will create a generation that both hits the target and achieves the purpose." The statement from the Prime Minister not specify the number of government officials participating in the training, its duration, or the full range of activities included in the program. somalia.content: Somalia Faces Mounting Security and Political Pressures as Foreign Troops Prepare to Withdraw Latest Headlines Somalia Faces Mounting Security and Political Pressures as Foreign Troops Prepare to Withdraw Somalia: Puntland Enlists Troops for US Training at Bosaso Military Base Mo Ibrahim Warns African Leaders Are Increasingly Embracing Authoritarian Rule UN Staff Evacuated From Somalia to Kenya After UNTMIS Closure US places Somalia on list of ports failing anti-terrorism security standards Advertise with us Home News Puntland Somalia World Sports Press Releases Somaliland Videos Opinion Contact Privacy Policy English Somali Somalia Faces Mounting Security and Political Pressures as Foreign Troops Prepare to Withdraw Staff Reporter GAROWE ONLINE Posted On 02-11-2026, 07:56PM MOGADISHU — Somalia's federal government is facing mounting security and political challenges as foreign troops prepare to withdraw from key positions in the country's Lower Shabelle region, raising concerns about a potential security vacuum and renewed instability. The African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), particularly Ugandan forces, is preparing to pull troops from several areas in Lower Shabelle and consolidate its presence around the Halane compound in Mogadishu, according to a report citing diplomatic correspondence. A letter sent to Western embassies, contains security warnings and outlines preparations for possible developments over the next 120 days. The correspondence points to growing concerns about the country's security situation as international forces reduce their presence outside the capital. Uganda is among the largest troop contributors to AUSSOM, which supports Somali security forces in operations against Al-Shabaab and efforts to stabilise areas recovered from the militant group. The planned redeployment comes as Somalia faces a prolonged political dispute between President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's administration and opposition groups over constitutional changes and the electoral process ahead of the 2027 elections. The political tensions have also intensified following efforts by the president to build support among political and traditional constituencies, while members of the opposition-led Somali Future Council continue to challenge the government's proposed electoral arrangements. According to the report, Hassan has sent two senior officials from the security and judicial institutions to engage with opposition figures who share power arrangements with the government. He reportedly warned that pursuing an alternative political structure could lead to the relocation of the country's capital, urging political actors to support his position. The remarks could further complicate relations between the government and the Somali Future Council, an opposition alliance that includes prominent former leaders and representatives of federal member states. The council has also faced criticism over its decision to open discussions with military officials representing the president, despite the government's continued commitment to its proposed electoral process. The report said the opposition's decision to engage in the talks, without securing changes to the government's position on the electoral framework, had raised questions about its negotiating strategy. The security situation in South West State is adding to the pressure on the federal government. Key bridges near Buurhakaba, along the route connecting the town to Mogadishu, have reportedly been cut, potentially complicating the movement of troops and supplies. The developments come after federal forces withdrew from positions around Leego, while some troops who left the area have reportedly been reluctant to return to the battlefield. The situation in South West has been marked by tensions between forces aligned with the federal government and those loyal to former regional president Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Lafta-Gareen, with control of strategic towns and military positions remaining a major point of contention. The combination of the planned foreign troop redeployment, political divisions and instability in South West State presents a significant challenge for Hassan's administration as Somalia prepares for a sensitive electoral period. The reported diplomatic warnings covering the next 120 days highlight growing international concern about the potential consequences of overlapping political and security crises. somalia.content: Pirates hijack Iranian fishing vessel off Somalia’s northeastern coast - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Pirates hijack Iranian fishing vessel off Somalia’s northeastern coast Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Monday November 2, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) – Armed pirates have hijacked an Iranian fishing vessel off Somalia’s northeastern coast, raising concerns that it could be used as a mothership to launch attacks on larger commercial ships. The European Union Naval Force’s Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean (MSCIO) said the pirates boarded the vessel, named Azini, at around 0900 UTC near coordinates 09°42’N, 053°55’E, approximately 185 nautical miles east of Bandarbayla, Somalia. The safety of the crew remained unknown. An officer with Puntland’s maritime police told The Associated Press that 12 pirates had seized the vessel and its 23 crew members, including 21 Iranian fishermen and two Somali security guards. MSCIO said the Azini matched the profile of vessels Somali pirates have previously used as motherships. Such vessels provide pirates with mobile bases from which to launch attacks on larger merchant ships farther offshore, beyond the operating range of smaller speedboats. By Saturday, the vessel had moved approximately 110 nautical miles farther east to coordinates 09°47’N, 055°45’E, bringing it closer to a major commercial shipping route. MSCIO reiterated its warning that the fishing vessel could be used as a pirate mothership. The hijacking comes amid renewed concerns over piracy off Somalia, following several years of relative calm. In August 2026, Turkish naval forces and the Somali National Armed Forces rescued the cargo vessel MV LATUF after it was hijacked off the Somali coast, according to Somalia’s Defence Ministry. The ministry said four boats used by the pirates were destroyed and 14 pirates were killed during the joint operation. It added that sustained pressure from security forces forced the remaining pirates to abandon the vessel. Security forces subsequently took control of the ship, which resumed its voyage safely, the ministry said. The operation was conducted under a defence cooperation agreement between Somalia and Türkiye, which provides a framework for cooperation in protecting Somalia’s coastline and combating maritime piracy. Somalia experienced a major wave of piracy between 2008 and 2018, with armed groups targeting commercial vessels and demanding ransoms. Attacks declined significantly for several years before re-emerging in late 2023 amid heightened security tensions in the region. For feedback, please contact translation@repubblica.it | Vai alla versione in italiano Read in English Italian Cooperation funding totalling €3.75 million, distributed across two geographical tranches for emergency interventions 02 November 2026 at 20:48 3 min read Rome – Somalia is facing a structural humanitarian crisis, exacerbated by a deadly combination of recurrent droughts, an internal armed conflict, displacement and a drastic reduction in international funding, according to the website of Info-cooperazione , the portal for Italian humanitarian workers. According to the Somalia Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan 2026 , over 4.8 million people are in urgent need of assistance to survive: food, along with basic necessities such as drinking water, hygiene kits and portable toilets to help prevent the spread of cholera. Furthermore: medical care, medicines, tents and materials to build shelters. And then there is the protection of people who have suffered physical or psychological violence. Funding from Italian Development Cooperation. The Nairobi office of the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation ( AICS ) has published a Call for Proposals to fund emergency interventions in Somalia. The available resources amount to €3.75 million, distributed across two geographical lots, with a maximum project duration of 24 months. READ THE CALL FOR APPLICATIONS More than 5 million people do not regularly eat nutritious food. The latest analysis, based on first-hand information and carried out last September, tells us that 5.1 million people are facing acute food insecurity , with projections indicating this figure will rise to 5.4 million by the end of the year. Living in a state of acute food insecurity means not having access to sufficient quantities of nutritious food in a safe and sustained manner, to the extent that one’s life is at risk. This figure is 50 per cent higher than in the same period in 2025. Around 1.92 million children aged between 6 and 59 months require treatment for acute malnutrition. The crisis is further exacerbated by cuts to global humanitarian funding, which have already led to the closure of 233 nutrition centres and 380 healthcare facilities. Objectives and areas of intervention. The initiative is divided into two geographical lots with overlapping sectors of intervention: water, sanitation, environment and land use; natural resource management and climate change adaptation; agriculture and food safety; health and nutrition. The causes of a never-ending civil war. In Somalia, in fact, there has been an uninterrupted internal war for 40 years now, since 1986. A conflict that has accompanied the gradual, now almost total, erosion of state institutions and has exacerbated the country’s age-old tribal fragmentation, amongst the numerous fundamentalist militias, federal governments lacking real power, and the so-called ‘warlords’, who are, in essence, nothing more than tribal chiefs who control a territory through private military forces and loyal militiamen, operating entirely outside any state or institutional chain of command. The various phases of the Somali conflict. From 1986 to 1991, an internal armed uprising emerged in opposition to the regime of President Siad Barre, who had been in power continuously since 1969, culminating in his flight from Mogadishu in January 1991. Siad Barre was initially an advocate of ‘Islamic/scientific socialism’ , under which he promoted major reforms such as the creation of a written alphabet for the Somali language, large-scale literacy campaigns, and fostered women’s emancipation and the formal fight against tribalism and corruption. But he then turned his attention to the United States, particularly during (and after) the disastrous war against Ethiopia. The onset of anarchy and clan-based conflicts. Like a film we have seen before, but also afterwards, once Barre’s regime had fallen, Somalia plunged into absolute and devastating anarchy, where various tribal groups and different ethnic factions drove the situation to the point of the catastrophic international intervention by the UN and the United States (UNOSOM and UNITAF) , remembered for the Battle of Mogadishu in 1993. Between 2006 and 2009, the Islamic Courts came to power. The rise of the Union of Islamic Courts and its control of Mogadishu led to military intervention by Ethiopia, with international support, to re-establish a transitional government. And so we come to the present day. With a federal government embroiled in a debilitating struggle against Al-Shabaab, an Islamist armed group linked to Al-Qaeda and harbouring cells of the so-called Islamic State within its ranks. All this means that Somalia is now a state where 54.4 per cent of the population lives below the poverty line, on less than $2.06 a day, a state that is only formally federal, but in reality divided into entities with varying degrees of autonomy or claims to independence, such as Somaliland (which has declared itself independent since 1991) and Puntland , as well as other semi-autonomous regions such as Jubaland. Many areas in the south and centre are under the influence and operational control of Al-Shabaab militias, which regularly carry out attacks on institutions in the capital with complete impunity. According to the Somalia Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan 2026, over 4.8 million people urgently require assistance, including food, clean water, hygiene supplies, and medical care. The situation is exacerbated by significant cuts in international funding, leading to the closure of numerous healthcare and nutrition centers. Currently, 5.1 million people are experiencing acute food insecurity, with projections indicating this could rise to 5.4 million by year-end. The country has been embroiled in civil war for over 40 years, resulting in the erosion of state institutions and the rise of tribal factions and militias, including Al-Shabaab. With more than half the population living below the poverty line, urgent intervention is needed to address the escalating crisis and provide essential support to those affected.
